name: Collapsing glomerulopathy
aliases: collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: An aggressive glomerular disease defined by segmental or global collapse of the glomerular tuft with overlying podocyte hyperplasia and hypertrophy
Presents with heavy, often massive, proteinuria, rapidly declining renal function and prominent tubulointerstitial injury with microcystic tubular dilatation
Strongly linked to APOL1 high-risk genotypes in people of African ancestry, and to viral triggers including HIV and parvovirus B19
HIV-associated nephropathy is the archetypal viral form, but the pattern also follows other infections, interferon and pamidronate exposure, and autoimmune disease
Podocytes show a dysregulated, dedifferentiated proliferative phenotype rather than the quiescent injured podocyte of classic FSGS
It is regarded as a distinct, more severe entity than other FSGS variants and warrants a search for a reversible trigger

Management combines treatment of any underlying cause (antiretroviral therapy in HIV, drug withdrawal, control of autoimmune disease) with immunosuppression/corticosteroids in idiopathic cases and supportive renal care
reference.pathophysiology: Collapsing glomerulopathy is a podocytopathy in which a severe injury drives podocytes to lose their differentiated markers and proliferate, forming a hyperplastic cap over a collapsed, wrinkled glomerular basement membrane. APOL1 high-risk variants render podocytes susceptible, and a 'second hit' such as viral infection, interferon exposure or another stressor precipitates the collapsing response. The intense podocyte injury produces massive proteinuria, while associated severe tubular injury with microcyst formation contributes to the rapid loss of function. The combination of tuft collapse and epithelial proliferation distinguishes it histologically from other FSGS variants and accounts for its worse prognosis.
additionalDifferentials: Acute tubular injury with heavy proteinuria
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy showing tuft collapse with podocyte hyperplasia and tubular microcysts
HIV and parvovirus B19 testing and broader viral screen
APOL1 genotyping in patients of African ancestry
Review of drug exposures including interferon and bisphosphonates
Autoimmune serology where a connective-tissue disease is suspected
Quantification of proteinuria and monitoring of renal function
redFlags: Rapid progression to advanced renal failure over weeks to months
Nephrotic-range or massive proteinuria with severe hypoalbuminaemia
Newly diagnosed HIV or other precipitating infection
Exposure to interferon or other implicated drugs
reference.prognosis: Collapsing glomerulopathy carries the worst prognosis among FSGS patterns, with rapid progression to end-stage kidney disease in many patients despite treatment. Outcomes are better when a reversible trigger such as HIV or an offending drug is identified and addressed early, but APOL1-associated idiopathic disease often responds poorly to immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Treating it as ordinary FSGS and underestimating its aggressiveness
Failing to test for HIV, parvovirus and other viral triggers
Overlooking implicated drugs such as interferon and bisphosphonates
Not considering APOL1 risk in patients of African ancestry
Delaying antiretroviral therapy in HIV-associated disease
management: Identify and treat a reversible trigger - antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated disease, treatment of parvovirus B19, and withdrawal of interferon or pamidronate
Renin-angiotensin system blockade with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker to reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure
Corticosteroids with or without additional immunosuppression for idiopathic disease, recognising the limited response
Supportive management of nephrotic syndrome with diuretics for oedema and a statin for dyslipidaemia
Close monitoring of proteinuria and renal function with early planning for dialysis or transplantation given rapid progression
APOL1 genotyping in patients of African ancestry with genetic counselling where relevant
Nephrology referral for biopsy-guided diagnosis and management
